Senses.Explanation: To receive binding precepts from a precept-giver, commonly as a dated event in a master’s biography: a lamp record says Huike served Bodhidharma for nine years and later received the precepts at Jizhou. It is also a public act. The Platform Record places Huineng on the high seat to confer formless precepts and tells the whole assembly, ‘each must receive the formless precepts in your own person’ (總須自體與受無相戒). The corpus does not leave the compound as ceremony alone. Yongjue’s precept-bestowal address asks, ‘What is a precept? How is a precept received?’ (云何為戒？戒云何受？), and later rebukes those who ‘have the name of receiving precepts but entirely lack the reality of receiving precepts’ (但取受戒之名，全無受戒之實). Juelang Sheng states that recipients and non-recipients are far apart and that receiving without keeping is an offense. Thus Chan records retain formal biographical and public reception while applying an explicit name-versus-reality test and linking reception to subsequent keeping.
Senses.Note: The entry describes a formal event and the record’s explicit test of name against reality. Exact count: 658 hits in 157 files.

AlternateTargets: Zhaozhou's 'a dog has no buddha-nature' case
the dog has no buddha-nature saying
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'a dog has no buddha-nature.' The corpus records 427 occurrences in 119 allowed texts; 228 add the noun 'saying' (話), and 91 explicitly prefix Zhaozhou's name. The phrase serves as a title or shorthand for the recorded exchange in which someone asks whether a dog has buddha-nature and Zhaozhou answers 'no.' Dahui's verse heading states 'Zhaozhou: a dog has no buddha-nature' (趙州狗子無佛性) and immediately restates the exchange as 'someone asked about a dog's buddha-nature; Zhaozhou answered, no' (有問狗佛性。趙州答曰無). Other records raise 'the saying that a dog has no buddha-nature' (狗子無佛性話), quote its word 'no' (無字), use it in questioning, and place it beside the separately attested wording 'a dog has buddha-nature' (狗子有佛性). The word 'no' is translated as English 'no.'
Senses.Note: No direct definition formula of the forms 'X is,' 'what is called X,' or 'what is X' was found, except one later question, 'What is “a dog has no buddha-nature”?' (如何是狗子無佛性), answered 'fishing' (釣). The term's stable corpus function is instead visible in headings, raised-case labels, verses, questions, and later reports about Zhaozhou's recorded case. The full earlier exchange and the later compound title are related evidence, not two meanings.
